report:
Based on the retrieved evidence, the answer is a qualified "yes" — but with important caveats about the strength and consistency of evidence.

**Strongest evidence: Bangladesh RCT.** The largest randomized controlled trial on community masking, involving 600 villages, found that mask promotion increased mask-wearing and reduced symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence, particularly with surgical masks. Effects were more pronounced in older adults (35% reduction in those 60+, 23% in those 50-60), while overall symptomatic-illness reduction was around 12% (https://theconversation.com/evidence-shows-that-yes-masks-prevent-covid-19-and-surgical-masks-are-the-way-to-go-167963). Yale researchers described this as the first randomized evidence that community masking reduces COVID-19 (https://macmillan.yale.edu/stories/first-randomized-study-shows-masks-reduce-covid-19-infections).

**Modeling supports population-level benefit.** A US-based modeling study found that even modestly effective masks, worn by a majority of the population, meaningfully reduce cumulative infections, peak infections, hospitalizations, and deaths — for example, 75% adoption of 50%-effective masks reduced infection attack rates substantially (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348860105_High-Quality_Masks_Reduce_Infections_and_Deaths_in_the_US). The PNAS evidence review similarly concludes that widespread mask use, combined with population effects (source control plus some wearer protection), can meaningfully reduce transmission at the community level (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2014564118).

**Caveats.** The Cochrane review of RCTs found only low-to-moderate confidence evidence, with modest and sometimes inconsistent effects on individual infection risk, though it did not evaluate population-level mandates specifically (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD006207_do-physical-measures-such-hand-washing-or-wearing-masks-stop-or-slow-down-spread-respiratory-viruses).

**Conclusion:** The best available randomized and modeling evidence supports that widespread mask-wearing can reduce COVID-19 transmission at a population level, though individual protective effects are more modest and evidence quality varies across contexts and mask types.
